meta.title: Who really said "Ask for work. If they do not give you work, ask for bread. If they do not give you bread, then take bread"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Emma Goldman, Union Square, 21 August 1893 — but the popular wording is trimmed. What the 1893 and 1911 printings actually say, and why there's no transcript.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Ask for work. If they do not give you work, ask for bread. If they do not give you bread, then take bread'?
meta.ogDescription: Emma Goldman said it at Union Square in 1893 and went to prison for it. But every surviving version is secondhand — and two words are missing.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Goldman said something very close to this to a mass meeting of striking cloakmakers and unemployed workers in Union Square, New York, on 21 August 1893 — the speech that led to her conviction for inciting to riot. But no transcript survives: the two early printings both end “if they do not give you work or bread, then take bread,” and Goldman’s own memoir remembers the sentence differently again, so this tidy popular form cannot be pinned to any primary text.

source.heading: Where the words are actually printed

source.excerpt: She delivered an impassioned speech, picturing in fiery words the misery of the wage slave’s life, and quoted the famous maxim of Cardinal Manning: “Necessity knows no law, and the starving man has a natural right to a share of his neighbor’s bread.” She concluded her exhortation with the words: “Ask for work. If they do not give you work, ask for bread. If they do not give you work or bread, then take bread.”
trail: 21 August 1893 — Goldman addresses a mass demonstration in Union Square, New York. She is arrested soon after in Philadelphia, convicted of inciting a riot, and sentenced to a year in prison (First Amendment Encyclopedia ↗).

1893 — Voltairine de Cleyre’s lecture In Defense of Emma Goldman and the Right of Expropriation puts the sentence at the head of its text: “Ask for work; if they do not give you work ask for bread; if they do not give you work or bread then take bread” (Marxists Internet Archive ↗).

1911 — Hippolyte Havel’s “Biographic Sketch,” printed at the front of Goldman’s Anarchism and Other Essays, gives the fullest early account: the Manning maxim first, then the sentence, with the same “work or bread” ending (Wikisource ↗).
1931 — In her autobiography Goldman recalls the moment herself, and the wording shifts: the crowd is told to demand work, then bread, and to take bread if denied both (Wikipedia ↗).
source.excerptNote: Havel’s sketch is a report, not a transcript — and note the third clause: work or bread, the two words the popular version drops.
source.rightsNote: The wording quoted here comes from two works published long before 1931 and free of US copyright: Voltairine de Cleyre’s 1893 lecture and Hippolyte Havel’s “Biographic Sketch” in the 1911 second revised edition of Anarchism and Other Essays, both freely readable online. Goldman’s own retelling in Living My Life (1931) is a separate matter — that book is still under US copyright in 2026, which is why this page describes its version rather than reprinting it.

author.name: Emma Goldman
author.heading: Who was Emma Goldman?
author.bio: Emma Goldman was among the most famous — and most surveilled — radicals in American public life, a lecturer and essayist whose speeches on labour, free speech and women’s autonomy drew crowds and police in roughly equal numbers. The Union Square address of August 1893 brought her a prison term: convicted of inciting to riot, she served ten months of a one-year sentence on Blackwell’s Island. Her writing survives in the collection Anarchism and Other Essays and, much later, in the autobiography Living My Life.

misattribution.heading: What gets garbled
misattribution.intro: No one else claims this line — Goldman is the right speaker. What goes wrong is the wording, and where people say it comes from.

items.why: Both early printings — de Cleyre’s 1893 lecture and Havel’s 1911 sketch — close with “if they do not give you work or bread, then take bread.” The form that circulates online drops those two words, flattening the escalation Goldman had just built (Wikisource ↗).

The sentence really does appear in that 1911 book — but in Hippolyte Havel’s biographical sketch, reporting a speech, not in any essay Goldman wrote. Quoting it as Goldman’s prose credits her with a sentence someone else set down (Project Gutenberg ↗).

Her own memoir recalls telling the crowd to demand work, then bread, and to take bread if denied both — a different verb and a different shape from the 1893 and 1911 printings. Two of the versions in circulation trace back to her; they do not match (Wikipedia ↗).

Her single most-quoted line — the one about not wanting a revolution she can’t dance at — is a modern paraphrase spun out of a passage in her memoir, not anything she actually wrote. Goldman attracts invented aphorisms, which is exactly why the genuine ones deserve a citation (Wikiquote ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The idea, and very likely the sentence, are genuinely Goldman’s — spoken in Union Square in August 1893 and printed by her comrades within months. But every surviving version is somebody’s report, and the neatest one is the least well attested (Wikisource ↗).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Havel’s sketch sets the scene plainly: the country was in the throes of a crisis, and thousands of unemployed crowded the streets of the large industrial centres. Goldman was one of the invited speakers at a Union Square demonstration of striking cloakmakers and the jobless, and she built to the line by first quoting Cardinal Manning — that necessity knows no law, and the starving man has a natural right to a share of his neighbour’s bread. Borrowing a cardinal’s authority before telling a hungry crowd to take bread was the rhetorical move, and it worked.

It also cost her. Days afterwards she was arrested in Philadelphia and brought back to New York on a charge of inciting to riot; a jury convicted her, and she served ten months of a one-year sentence on Blackwell’s Island (Wikipedia ↗). That prosecution is the reason the sentence is so well remembered and so poorly documented at the same time: what mattered legally was what witnesses said she said, and the surviving versions of that do not quite agree.
detailsBody: Goldman spoke from notes she abandoned on the spot — she recalled that the prepared text looked cold once she saw the crowd. What exists instead is a set of reports: newspaper accounts, police testimony at her trial, her comrades’ printed versions, and, nearly four decades later, her own memory. Where they converge is the escalation — work, then bread, then take it — and the Manning quotation that licensed it. Where they diverge is the verb and the final clause.

That is the honest shape of the evidence, and it is why this page says “attributed” rather than “verified.” The thought is unambiguously Goldman’s. The exact fourteen words in circulation are one editor’s tidy-up of a sentence that was already secondhand.
context.pull: “Necessity knows no law, and the starving man has a natural right to a share of his neighbor’s bread.” — Cardinal Manning, as Goldman quoted him first

sourcesVerified.claim: Hippolyte Havel's "Biographic Sketch" reports Goldman's Union Square speech, quotes Cardinal Manning's maxim, and concludes: "Ask for work. If they do not give you work, ask for bread. If they do not give you work or bread, then take bread."
The scanned page 25 of the 1911 second revised edition of Anarchism and Other Essays carries the Union Square passage and the "Ask for work... work or bread... take bread" sentence.
Project Gutenberg's full text of Anarchism and Other Essays contains the same Biographic Sketch passage with the Cardinal Manning maxim and the "work or bread" wording.

Voltairine de Cleyre's 1893 lecture In Defense of Emma Goldman and the Right of Expropriation prints the sentence as "Ask for work; if they do not give you work ask for bread; if they do not give you work or bread then take bread", both as an epigraph and again in the body.

Wikipedia dates the Union Square speech to 21 August 1893, gives Goldman's own recollection using "demand work / demand bread / take bread", notes the conflicting undercover-agent account, and records her arrest in Philadelphia, conviction for inciting to riot, one-year Blackwell's Island sentence and release after ten months; it also gives her dates as 27 June 1869 to 14 May 1940.
The First Amendment Encyclopedia states Goldman was convicted and sentenced to one year in prison for inciting a riot following an 1893 speech at Union Square, New York City.

Wikiquote's Emma Goldman page presents the "If I can't dance, I don't want to be part of your revolution" variants as popular paraphrases derived from a passage in Living My Life, not as a direct quotation from Goldman.
